⚰️ One Twin Dies — when is the father exempt?
🏠 Father Dies First — do the heirs still owe the priest?
💰 'Five, Not Half of Five' — R' Meir and R' Yehuda's monetary dispute
👩‍👩‍👦 Two Wives, Two Sons Intermingled — ten sela and its complications

overview.title: 📖 Overview: When Twins Blur the Firstborn
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 48a–48b
overview.hebrewSource: מִי שֶׁלֹּא בִּכְּרָה אִשְׁתּוֹ וְיָלְדָה שְׁנֵי זְכָרִים — נוֹתֵן חָמֵשׁ סְלָעִים לְכֹהֵן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf's new mishna addresses a wife's first pregnancy that produces twin boys: since one of them is definitely a firstborn but no one knows which, the father owes five sela after 30 days regardless. The Gemara probes what happens if the father dies first — do the sons, as heirs, still owe the debt, and does it matter whether they already divided the estate? This spins into a debate about whether 'a loan written in the Torah' can be collected from liened property already sold, and whether the mitzva requires exactly five sela or accepts partial payment. The daf then turns to two wives who each bore a son that became intermingled, generating a parallel set of complications for two priests instead of one.

slides.subtitle: How much is owed when a firstborn's identity is uncertain

Perhaps the one who died was the firstborn

slides.title: 🏠 Why Does Dividing the Estate Matter?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara narrows the mishna to a case within 30 days of birth

nodes.content: ❓ If the father died after 30 days, the property is already liened for the mitzva — dividing shouldn't matter at all
💡 So the mishna must mean the father died WITHIN 30 days — the obligation attaches to the sons themselves, not yet to the property
🤝 Rabbi Yirmeya: like two men both named Yosef ben Shimon who jointly own a field — a creditor of either can collect from it, since he's owed by one of them either way
⚖️ Rava's answer: brothers who divide inherited property are half-heirs, half-purchasers (Rav Asi) — and an oral Torah debt collects only from heirs, not purchasers (Rav Pappa)

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Once divided, the priest can collect only half the debt — the half where the sons remain 'heirs' rather than 'purchasers' from each other.

slides.title: 💰 Five Sela — Or Half of Five?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda locate their true disagreement

lines.speaker: R' Meir
lines.text: The Torah requires giving specifically five sela — never half or part of five. If only two-and-a-half sela are available from the property, we take nothing.

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: The Torah's five sela can be given even in part — two-and-a-half sela of liened property is still collectible.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But a baraita has R' Yehuda requiring ten dinars specifically from each brother's inherited share — doesn't that show he also needs the full five?

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Both agree on 'five, not half of five' — their real dispute is Rav Asi's rule about heirs-vs-purchasers, which R' Yehuda rejects entirely.

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: R' Yehuda holds the whole five sela remains collectible from the divided estate because he does not accept that division makes brothers into purchasers from each other.

slides.title: 👩‍👩‍👦 Two Wives, One Confused Pair of Sons
slides.subtitle: The mishna extends the uncertainty to two separate priests

boxes.title: Both Give to One Priest
items: 10 sela given for two intermingled firstborns
If one son dies within 30 days: priest returns 5 sela
Each mother's son is certainly her own firstborn

boxes.title: Each Gives to a Different Priest
items: If one son then dies, neither priest returns anything
Each priest claims: 'I received payment for the surviving child'
The father cannot recover from either possession

boxes.title: Mixed Combinations
items: Male + female (either mother): 5 sela owed — one is certainly firstborn
Two females + one male, or 2+2: nothing owed — female may have come first each time

slides.title: 🔀 Why Can't the Priest Just Reject Each Claimant?
slides.subtitle: Rava's guarantor analogy resolves the two-priest puzzle

steps.content: 1️⃣ Question: why can't each father say to each priest, 'go collect from the other one instead'?
2️⃣ Rava: a person's own property is his own guarantee — one cannot claim from a guarantor when one could have claimed from the debtor directly
3️⃣ Yet the mishna clearly lets the priest collect from divided property even when he can't identify which brother owes him
4️⃣ Answer: Rabbi Yirmeya's joint-field precedent shows a creditor CAN collect from either partner precisely because he's owed by one of the two

callout.label: Two versions:
callout.text: The Gemara records a first version built around brothers who bought a shared field, and a second (48b) built around one Yosef ben Shimon selling to the other — reaching the same halakhic conclusion.

summary.principle: When it is certain that a firstborn exists somewhere among uncertain candidates, the five-sela obligation still applies — but its collectability from an estate depends on whether the sons are legally 'heirs' or 'purchasers' of the divided property.

flowSteps.content: 👬 Twin sons, wife's first pregnancy → 5 sela owed after 30 days regardless of which twin is firstborn
⚰️ If father dies within 30 days, obligation attaches to the sons; division of the estate then matters

columns.content: 💰 R' Meir: exempt once divided (2.5 sela isn't 'five'); R' Yehuda: still owed (rejects heirs/purchasers split)
👩‍👩‍👦 Two wives, two sons: 10 sela to one priest is returnable; to two priests, neither returns anything

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: an uncertain firstborn among certain candidates still generates a real, if complicated, monetary debt

quiz.q: If a wife's first pregnancy produces twin boys, what does the mishna require of the father?
o: Nothing, since it's uncertain which is firstborn
Ten sela to be safe
Five sela to the priest after 30 days
Five sela immediately at birth
quiz.e: Since one of the twins is certainly a firstborn even though it's unknown which, the father owes five sela to a priest once 30 days have passed.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara conclude the mishna's case of the father dying and sons disputing division must refer to death WITHIN 30 days of the twins' birth?
o: Because after 30 days sons are never obligated
Because after 30 days the property is already liened for the mitzva, so division would be irrelevant to R' Meir's ruling
Because the mishna says so explicitly
Because twins are always redeemed within 30 days
quiz.e: If the father died after 30 days, the redemption debt already attached to his property as a lien, so whether the sons later divided it should not matter — hence the Gemara reinterprets the case as death within 30 days.

quiz.q: What is Rav Asi's principle about brothers who divide an inherited estate?
o: They remain full heirs to the entire estate
They become purchasers from each other for the whole estate
With regard to half the property they are heirs, and with regard to the other half they are considered purchasers from each other
Division has no legal effect on inheritance
quiz.e: Rav Asi teaches that dividing brothers are, in effect, half heirs and half purchasers from one another — a distinction that matters because an oral Torah debt collects only from heirs' property, not purchasers'.

quiz.q: What is the actual point of disagreement between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda once the Gemara reinterprets the mishna?
o: Whether five sela can be given as five separate coins
Whether Rav Asi's heirs/purchasers division applies to reduce the collectible debt
Whether twins can ever be firstborns
Whether the mother's status affects the payment
quiz.e: Both tannaim actually agree that the Torah requires giving five sela and not half; their true dispute is whether Rav Asi's principle (that dividing brothers are half purchasers) limits what the priest can collect — R' Yehuda rejects it.

quiz.q: In the case of two wives whose sons became intermingled, why can the father not recover any money if he gave five sela to each of two different priests and one son then died?
o: Because the payments were never valid to begin with
Because each priest can claim the money he received was payment for the surviving child
Because two priests can never be paid for the same redemption
Because the mishna requires payment only to one priest
quiz.e: Since each priest holds his own five sela and can insist he was paid for whichever son survived, the father cannot demonstrate that either specific priest received payment for the deceased son.
